title: CLR/78/2011 of SHER MOHAMMAD Vs VINOD PRAKASH

paras.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Civil Revision No. 78 of 2011
Sher Mohammad. ........Revisionist
 Versus
Vinod Prakash. .......Respondent
Mr. Sudhir Kumar, Advocate for the revisionist.
Mr. S.K. Posti, Advocate for respondent.
Dated: August 12, 2013
Hon'ble V.K. Bist, J.

This revision has been filed by the revisionist/
tenant against the judgment and decree dated 11.10.2011
passed by the learned District Judge, Nainital in S.C.C.
No. 5 of 1984 'Smt. Chandra Bhaga Vs. Sher Mohammad'
whereby the suit for eviction, arrears of rent and damages
was decreed with cost in favour of the plaintiff
(respondent herein).
 Precisely stated that the property in dispute is a
shop in which the revisionist was a tenant of Smt.
Chandra Bhaga-the landlady. The landlady filed a suit for
ejectment and recovery of arrears of rent and damages
against the revisionist after serving upon the revisionist a
notice of demand and termination of tenancy alleging that
the revisionist has not paid the rent since 01.08.1974. The
revisionist contested the suit and filed his written
statement contending that he has paid the rent to the
landlady who has not issued the receipts therefor. The
revisionist, after receiving the notice of demand, in order
to save his tenancy, offered the landlady entire amount
claimed by her but she refused to accept the same.
Thereafter, the revisionist remitted the amount through
money orders, which too was not received by the

2
landlady, and as such, the revisionist deposited the
amount in the Court of Munsif, Haldwani under Section
30 of the U.P. Act XIII of 1972. On these submissions, the
revisionist claimed that he was not in arrears of rent on
the date of filing of the suit, and as such, the suit was
liable to be dismissed. The respondent-Vinod Prakash
examined himself as attorney of the plaintiff-landlady.
The revisionist examined himself to prove his case. The
parties also lead documentary evidence. The learned
District Judge, by judgment and decree dated 28.5.1990,
decreed the suit. Aggrieved by the judgment and decree,
the revisionist preferred a revision before High Court,
Allahabad bearing Civil Revision No. 692 of 1996. After
hearing the parties, the revision was allowed and the
judgment and decree of the Court below was set aside and
the matter was remanded to the Court below for decision
afresh. A review application was moved by the landlady
before the High Court, Allahabad against the judgment
dated 21.05.1993. The said review application was
rejected by the High Court, Allahabad by order dated
04.01.2010. Thereafter, the learned Court below
proceeded with the case. During the pendency of the
review application, the plaintiff-landlady died and the
respondent was substituted in place of the plaintiff-landlady as her sole legal representative in the suit before
the learned Court below. The learned District Judge has
again passed a decree for eviction of the revisionist from
the premises in dispute vide impugned judgment and
order dated 11.10.2011 and the revisionist, being
aggrieved by the said decision, has come up in this
revision.

3
 I have heard Mr. Sudhir Kumar, Advocate for the
revisionist, Mr. S.K. Posti, Advocate for respondent and
perused the material available on record.
 The material point involved in this revision is as to
whether the defendant/tenant is in arrears of rent and is
liable to pay damages to the plaintiff/landlord and
whether the tenant/revisionist has committed any default
in making payment of rent and has failed to make
payment of the arrears of rent within the period of notice
of demand to the landlady/plaintiff.
 Mr. Sudhir Kumar, learned counsel for the tenant/
revisionist first of all argued that it is admitted fact that
the notice of demand was issued on 26.8.1983 and was
sent to the revisionist by post and is said to have been
served on 30.8.1983. The period of notice of demand is
one month as provided in clause (a) of sub-section (2) of
Section 20 of the Act XIII of 1972. The period of notice
expired on 30.09.1983. It is pleaded on behalf of the
revisionist that though the defendant had paid the rent to
the plaintiff, still in order to avoid legal complications and
save his tenancy went to the plaintiff personally and
tendered the whole amount, but she and her husband
refused to take the amount, hence the defendant sent the
whole amount demanded by the plaintiff i.e. ` 14,925.00
by money order on 27.09.1983. However, the plaintiff
deliberately avoided accepting the same, inasmuch as, her
husband falsely informed the tendering postman that the
plaintiff is out of station. Even if it is presumed that the
plaintiff was not available when the money order was
tendered to the plaintiff, it was her duty to make
arrangement for the receipt of the rent. She made herself
deliberately scarce. The husband of the plaintiff, however,
later on after expiry of the period, took intimation, but did

4
not come to the post office to receive the same. It is
contended that a huge amount could not be handed over
to the postman and his duty was only to intimate her or
her agent about the money order. Neither plaintiff nor her
husband came to demand the amount of the money order
from the post office, therefore, the defendant is not in
arrears of rent because he took the action by remitting the
whole amount demanded in the notice. After the money
order was received back by the defendant, he deposited
the amount in the court of Munsif, Haldwani District
Nainital on 08.o9.1983 under section 30 of the U.P. Act
No. 13 of 1972. So in any case, the plaintiff cannot be said
to be a defaulter or in arrears of rent. It is contended that
the defendant has, however, tendered the rent to the
plaintiff personally but she refused to take the same and
she also avoided to take the money order sent to her by
the defendant.
 Learned counsel for the revisionist relied upon the
case of 'Sri Sidheshwari Prasad Agarwal Vs. Sri Gauri
Shankar', reported in 1977 ARC 311, in which the full
bench held that "Thus, a tenant, who remitted the rent
claimed, through a money order within the time
prescribed in the notice, could not be held to have
committed a default under Section 3(1)(a) of U.P. Act III
of 1947 once he had sent the amount within time. Bhikha
Lal's case (supra) fully covers the instant case. He
contended that the Court below made an observation that
the tenant should have sent the money order to the
plaintiff and the money order sent to the counsel of the
landlord is a sufficient discharge of the obligation.
 The revisionist further relied upon a decision of
Hon'ble High Court, Allahabad in the case of 'Badri
Prasad Vs. District Judge, Gonda and others', reported in

5
1982 ARC 394 wherein the High Court has held as
follows:-
"In view of the above definition the opposite
parties can be said to have failed to pay only if
it can be said that they neglected to do
something which they were expected to do or
they left some possible or expected action
unperformed. In the case on hand, on receipt
of notice of demand the action expected from
the opposite parties was to tender rent to the
petitioner either personally or through some
agency recognized by law. Post Office is a
commonly recognized agency for carrying
money from the remitter to the payee.
Therefore, when on receipt of the notice of
demand of rent the opposite parties remitted
the rent through money order to the
petitioner, they took the action expected of
them. They cannot be said to have failed to
take action which they were required to take
under Section 20(2)(a) of the Act."
 Learned counsel for the revisionist contended that it
is fully established on record that after the landlady had
refused to accept the rent, the revisionist has remitted the
entire amount of arrears of rent as claimed by the
landlady through money orders within the period of the
notice. He submitted that it is established on record that
after the money order was returned by the Post Office, the
revisionist deposited the amount in the Court of Munsif,
Haldwani under Section 30 of the Act XIII of 1972 well
before the suit was filed. The plaintiff/ respondent has not
explained the manner in which the amount could have
been paid by the revisionist to the respondent before
filing of the suit. He submitted that the revisionist was left
with no other option except to deposit the rent in Court
under Section 30 of the Act XIII of 1972 when the
landlady refused to accept the amount of rent when
offered to her in cash by the revisionist and also refused to

6
accept the amount when remitted by money order by the
revisionist. He submitted that the plaintiff/landlady
cannot be allowed to take benefit of her own unjust and
malafide actions. She refused to accept the rent when
tendered to her by the tenant; she did not claim money
order when presented to her by the Post Office; she has
filed the suit alleging the tenant to be defaulter and she
cannot be permitted to claim the tenant to be a defaulter
particularly when she herself had refused to accept the
rent. He contended that the revisionist has deposited the
amount claimed in the notice under Section 30 of the Act
XIII of 1972, before filing of the suit, and all rents for the
period subsequent to that period, till the passing of the
decree have already been deposited in the Court, no
decree for ejectment of the revisionist or even for recovery
of arrears of rent could be passed. He further contended
that the revisionist has admitted the receipts issued to
him, but in order to judge the correctness of the receipts,
it is necessary to have a look on the said receipt book,
because it is apparent that the receipts have not been
issued in a regular course but they had been issued at the
leisure of the landlady. Receipts for four-five months are
issued, at a time, for each month separately. The receipts
are also not in regular order of the dates of issue. This
supports the case of the revisionist that though the rent
was realized, but the receipts were issued much after. The
witness of the plaintiff/landlady has not explained the
circumstances in which the receipts were not issued in a
regular course. This also creates doubts about the
correctness of the case of the plaintiff/landlady and much
importance cannot be placed on the rent receipt book.
 Learned counsel for the revisionist further
submitted that in the case in hand the power of attorney is

7
alleged to have been executed on 04.07.1984, after filing
of the suit and no act has been done by the attorney on the
basis of such power of attorney. The alleged power of
attorney is neither registered nor has been authenticated
and verified by any Notary Public or any Judge or
Magistrate. Section 85 of the Evidence Act provides that
there shall be a presumption in respect of power of
attorneys executed and authenticated before a Notary
Public or a Judge or a Magistrate. If a power of attorney is
not executed and authenticated by a Notary Public or
Judge or Magistrate, no presumption of its execution and
authentication can be made. He submitted that there is
another aspect also. Rules 1 and 2 of Order III of the Code
of Civil Procedure provide that a suit can be instituted by
an agent, duly appointed and recognized. It is submitted
that in view of the above provisions, a person holding a
power of attorney can do all acts on behalf of his
principal, but he cannot appear as a witness in lieu of his
principal. He submitted that the plaintiff/landlady had
herself done the acts required to be done by her and no
act was done by the alleged attorney on her behalf. This
statement further shows that the plaintiff/landlady could
have appear in the Court to tender her evidence. It also
shows that the witness has no personal knowledge of all
material facts, which are in exclusive knowledge of the
plaintiff/landlady. His statement, as to the acts done by
the plaintiff/landlady, is not admissible in evidence, being
hearsay evidence, as provided in Section 60 of the
Evidence Act. The revisionist relied upon the decision of
the Jammu Kashmir High Court in the case of 'Sant Ram
Vs. State', reported in AIR 1983 S.C. 906. He submitted
that the learned District Judge has failed to consider the
respective cases of the parties and has also failed to

8
consider the evidence on record in its proper perspective
and has also failed to decide the same in accordance with
law and the observations made by the High Court,
Allahabad in the remand order. The impugned judgment
and decree passed by the learned District Judge cannot be
sustained in law and is liable to be set aside.
 On the other hand, Mr. S.K. Posti, learned counsel
for the plaintiff/landlady submitted that the tenant Sher
Mohammad was inducted as a tenant in the year 1965, the
tenanted accommodation is a shop and the rent is ` 125/-
per month with water tax etc. He submitted that the
tenant purchased his own shop in the same market in the
year 1968 and let out the shop on rent which is now in
possession of the tenant himself and is doing the furniture
business over there. He submitted that suit was filed by
the landlady against the tenant under the Rent Control
Act for the need of her son, who became the lawyer and
wants to start his practice, and for that purpose he wants
to open his office/chamber in the shop, which was let out
to the tenant. He submitted that when tenant stopped
making payment of rent since from September, 1974 till
the 26.08.1983, the landlady compelled to file a suit of
recovery of rent and eviction against the tenant and the
prescribed authority vide order dated 28.04.1990 decreed
the suit and directed the tenant to hand over the
possession. Against the order of the prescribed authority,
the tenant preferred a revision before the Allahabad High
Court, who vide its judgment dated 21st May, 1993 set-aside the order of the prescribed authority and remanded
case back to the prescribed authority to decide afresh. He
submitted that earlier mode of the payment of rent was in
cash for which receipt was given by the landlady with a

9
counter signed receipt and when the tenant stopped
paying rent, the landlady requested the tenant several
time either to pay rent or vacate the shop but the tenant
did not pay rent. Thereafter, a notice was sent on
26.08.1983, which was served upon the tenant on
30.08.1983, which is an admitted fact. The tenant gave no
reply and did not tender the rent after receipt of the
notice. Since a period of one month as provided under
Section 20(2)(a) of Rent Control Act was expiring on
28.08.1983, the tenant sent a money order on 27.09.1983
from Haldwani Post Office, though the tenant and
landlord are living at Tanakpur and shop in question is
also at Tanakpur. He submitted that the prescribed
authorities have recorded a finding that the money order
send by the tenant from Haldwani Post Office was never
reached to the landlady nor the landlady was aware about
the sending of the money order. He submitted that the
notice was served upon tenant on 30.08.1983 and alleged
money order was sent on 27.09.1983. Ultimately rent was
deposited on 08.11.1983 but no interest and cost of the
suit was deposited as provided under Section 20(4) of the
Rent Control Act. He submitted that the tenant stated that
the landlord refused to accept the rent but contrary to it,
the tenant in his written statement, has stated that the
landlord avoided the rent but he never stated that the
landlord refused to accept the rent, which is a condition
president for deposit rent under Section 30 of the Act.
Contrary to it, the tenant in his application (paper No.
145C) stated that on 16.05.1984, he was at Delhi and came
back from Delhi on 19.05.1984. This statement was made
by the tenant on oath. But in a statement before the
prescribed authority (paper No. 98C/1), the tenant stated
that on 18.05.1984, he was at Munsif Court, Khatima

10
where his case under Section 30 of the Rent Control Act
was dismissed in default which was restored on his
application on same day. He submits that the whole case
of the tenant is based on fraud committed by him. He
submitted that the Munsif Court, Khatima vide order
dated 23.05.1985, in proceeding under Section 30 of the
Rent Act, directed the tenant to tender the money directly
to the landlady, which was never complied by the tenant.
 So far the question of sending rent through money
order is concerned, the tenant has stated that since the
rent was sent through money order within a period of 30
days from the date of the receipt of the notice, hence there
is no default on the part of the tenant and for this purpose
he relied upon a judgment of the Allahabad High Court
reported in AIR 1974 Allahabad-366. He argued that the
question referred before the above mentioned full bench
was whether on the fact and circumstances of the case, if
the tenant have sent the money order within time, which
had reached the landlord after the expiry of the 30 days,
could the tenant be said a defaulter, the full bench, after
relying the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the
case of 'Commissioner of Income Tax Bombay Vs. M/s.
Ogale Glass Works Ltd.', reported in AIR 1954 SC page
429 observed that if the money is sent to addressee
through post office, on his request, then the post office is
a agent of addressee and if there is no request then the
post office is agent of sender. He submitted that the full
bench in his judgment in paragraphs 7, 8, 13, 16, 18 and
19 has held that if request is from the side of the
addressee, then the post office is the agent of the
addressee otherwise not. He submitted that the above
mention view of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the
case of Commissioner of Income Tax Bombay Vs. M/s.

11
Ogale Glass Works Ltd. AIR 1954 SC page 429 was
reiterated in 36 ITR page 488 and 59 ITR page 738.
 Learned counsel for the plaintiff/respondent argued
that the tenant himself is saying that he is not availing the
benefit of section 20(4) of the Rent Control Act, meaning
thereby he is admitting that he had not deposited the rent
at the date of first hearing. The first date of hearing was
on 18.05.1984, the tenant failed to deposit the rent on that
day and even thereafter, he failed to deposit rent on
second date of hearing. He failed to deposit even at the
time of filing of his written statement but deposited on
07.11.1983 under Section 30 of the Rent Control Act.
Therefore, the benefit of the section 20(4) of the Rent
Control Act neither demanded by the tenant nor can be
granted to him.
 Learned counsel for the plaintiff/respondent then
submitted that the suit was filed on 2302.1984 and the
notice of demand was issued by the landlady on
26.08.1983, which was served upon tenant on 30.08.1983
and demanded rent was deposited on 07.11.1983 but the
tenant again failed to deposit the rent of 01.11.1983 to
31.07.1984 which was subsequently deposited on
11.07.1984. Therefore, at the time of filing of the suit, he
was again defaulter of 4 months and 9 months rent, which
was deposited by him in the Court on 11.07.1984 and he
was defaulter on this account also. Learned counsel for
the plaintiff relied on the judgment reported in 2009 (2)
ARC page 79, in which it was held that if any short fall in
deposit under Section 20(4) of the Rent Control Act, the
short fall in deposit cannot be condoned and strict
compliance is required. Further the Hon'ble Supreme
Court of India in the case reported in 2010 (3) ARC page
874 has held that the conduct of the tenant is also taken

12
into consideration and if the conduct of the tenant is
devious he is not entitled to any relief. He submitted that
in the present case, the conduct of the tenant is that the
tenant stopped payment of rent from September, 1974.
The deposit made by him was not a valid deposit.
Therefore, as held out by the trial Court, the tenant was
never regular in depositing rent during the pendency of
the suit and he used to deposit the rent after two years or
three years during the pendency of the suit. This conduct
of the tenant disentitles him from any relief of this Court.
He then argued that as per the contention of the tenant
that the landlady has not appeared and on her behalf her
power of attorney, her son Vinod Prakash appeared,
which is not permissible in law. In this regard he
submitted that Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case
reported in 2006 (3) Civil Court Cases- 456 held that the
attorney is competent to depose in respect of the all
matters except the matters, which are required to be done
personally by principal.
 Learned counsel for the plaintiff also submitted that
the tenant filed the revision petition against the order of
the trial Court and this Court, while entertaining the
revision petition, directed the tenant vide order dated
09.11.2011 to deposit the all decreetal amount within the
period of three weeks, which has never been complied
with by the tenant. The landlord filed a list of arrears,
which was outstanding against the tenant and was remain
un-rebutted, which shows that the decreetal amount, as
on 24.05.1911, is ` 1,59,588/-, but after the order passed
by this Court, the tenant only tendered ` 5,000/- by
moving an application before this Court, but not complied
the order passed by this Court, the tenant is defaulter on
this account also. He lastly contended that the tenant has

13
shown his address on invitation card as 'selection shoes
and furniture, main market Tanakpur', which shows that
he is doing business of the shoes and furniture from his
shop owned by him and the tenanted shop is not in use of
the tenant. He submitted that the conduct of the tenant
will also be visualized before this Court that he had not
deposited the rent from January to till date during the
pendency of revision petition before this Court. He
submitted that the tenant is not entitled to any relief from
this Court and he is liable to be evicted.
 I have considered the rival contentions of learned
counsel for the parties, have gone through the law cited by
them and have also minutely examined the judgment
passed by the trial Court.
 Clause (a) of sub-section (2) of Section 20 of the
U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and
Eviction) Act, 1972, provides protection to a tenant but
with certain condition. Same is being quoted here:
20. (2) A suit for the eviction of a tenant from
a building after the determination of his
tenancy may be instituted on one or more of
the following grounds, namely :
(a) that the tenant is in arrears of rent for not
less than four months, and has failed to pay
the same to the landlord within one month
from the date of service upon him of a notice
of demand:
Aforesaid provision provides protection to the
tenant who is in arrears of rent. A landlord can file a suit
for ejectment of a tenant after termination of the tenancy
of a tenant, who is in arrears of rent of more than four
months and has failed to pay the same within one month
from the date of receipt of the notice of demand. In the
present case, the rent is due since 01.08.1974; the notice
of demand was issued on 26.08.1983 and served on the

14
revisionist on 30.08.1983. Revisionist remitted the
arrears of rent through money order on 27.9.1983. When
the money orders were returned to the revisionist, the
revisionist deposited the entire rent in the Court of
Munsif, Haldwani on 08.11.1983. It is been contended by
the revisionist that there had been no default in payment
of rent and rent of more than four months was not due on
the date of the suit as he had deposited rent in Court
under Section 30 of the Act. In the case in hand, earlier
mode of the payment was cash and landlady used to issue
the receipt after receiving the rent in cash and the
landlady while issuing the notice dated 26.08.1983 again
stated, in para-4 of her notice, to pay the rent and obtain
the receipt. Para 4 of the notice is reproduced below:
"That you are hereby demanded to pay the
entire arrears of rent due as aforesaid within
one month of the date of receipt of this notice
to my client and obtain the receipt."
Therefore, in the present case neither there was an
agreement between the landlady and tenant to send the
rent through money order nor there was any previous
mode of the payment, by which it can be said that the rent
can be tendered through post office. Therefore, the case
reported in AIR 1974 Allahabad page 366 and 1982 ARC
394 are not applicable in this case and tenant is defaulter
and is liable to be evicted on the ground of the default.
 The lower Court has held that though after receiving
the legal notice of demand, the tenant paid the arrears of
rent, including tax, through money order and in order to
protect his right he deposited the rent under Section 30(1)
of U.P. Act No. XIII of 1972 in the Court, but he failed to
deposit the rent and tax regularly for each month during

15
the pendency of suit. The Court held that revisionist is
defaulter in making payment of rent and water tax
regularly. This finding is based on the papers filed by the
revisionist. I find this finding as correct finding.
 I do not find any illegality in the order of learned
District Judge.
 The revision is dismissed. No order as to costs.
 (V.K. Bist, J.)
 12.08.2013
NCM:
